rows.title: Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem to step down in June
rows.summary: Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem announced that he will not seek a second term when his seven-year term ends in June 2027. He took office on June 3, 2020, as the economy was rebounding from the first COVID lockdowns, and later led a 16-month run of rate hikes that began in March 2022 after inflation climbed toward its 8.1% peak. That campaign included a full one-percentage-point hike in July 2022 and took the key rate to 5% by July 2023, before cuts began in June 2024 and brought it down to 2.25% in October 2025. Facing a higher inflation outlook, the bank raised its rate again to 2.5% in October 2026. The bank's board has formed a search committee for his successor, and the federal government will have the final say on the appointment.
rows.fact: Macklem said he will leave when his term ends in June 2027, and the Bank of Canada's board has started a search for the next governor. Under him the policy rate rose from near zero to 5% between 2022 and 2023, was cut to 2.25% by October 2025, and was raised to 2.5% in October 2026.
rows.why: 중앙은행 총재 교체가 왜 중요한 경제 뉴스인지, 그리고 지난 6년간 캐나다가 금리를 어떻게 움직이며 물가와 싸웠는지 한눈에 볼 수 있습니다.
rows.why_en: It shows why a change at the top of a central bank matters, and traces how Canada used interest rates to fight inflation over the past six years.
rows.term_def: The short-term interest rate a central bank sets. Raising it makes borrowing more expensive, which cools spending and inflation; cutting it does the opposite.
rows.note: 7-day story (announced Nov. 16 ET). Departure date and search process cross-checked with The Canadian Press report via MoneySense and Canadian Mortgage Professional (search firm Egon Zehnder, decision expected by spring 2027).

opinion.title: Carmichael: Macklem is stepping aside after a career of consummate public service
opinion.author: Kevin Carmichael
opinion.summary: Economics columnist Kevin Carmichael looks back on Macklem's career, which began as a Bank of Canada researcher in 1984 and included work on inflation targeting. He notes that a 2021 review under Macklem kept the roughly 2% inflation target because no alternative was clearly better, and that the target was later renewed for five more years. Carmichael calls the full-point hike of July 2022 a bold move and argues Macklem was right to bet that plentiful job vacancies would soften the blow, while saying he probably waited too long to start raising rates after COVID. He also notes Macklem withstood political attacks and pushed on productivity, payments regulation and better forecasting tools. The column lists possible successors and suggests Prime Minister Carney likely already has a shortlist.
opinion.why: 한 중앙은행 총재의 결정들을 평가하면서, 금리 인상의 '타이밍'이 왜 그렇게 어려운지 생각해 볼 수 있는 칼럼입니다.
opinion.why_en: By judging one governor's record, the column helps you think about why timing interest rate moves is so difficult.

rows.title: Fed's Cook says rate hikes needed to lower high inflation
rows.summary: Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook said in a speech at the Central Bank of Chile's annual conference in Santiago that U.S. interest rates are not yet high enough to bring down inflation. She said the Fed's quarter-point hike in September was not enough and that data since then do not show inflation is on a sustainable path back to 2%. Cook was one of two officials who dissented in October when the Fed held its target range at 3.75% to 4.00%, and she warned that waiting could force bigger hikes later that would strain households and the financial system. She described growth as strong and accelerating, the job market as solid, and financial conditions as too loose to restrain demand. In her speech she noted PCE inflation of 3.8% and core PCE of 3.2% over the 12 months to October.
rows.fact: Cook said current policy is not restrictive enough and that the September rate hike was insufficient. She dissented in favour of a hike at the October meeting, when the Fed held rates at 3.75% to 4.00%, and said financial conditions remain accommodative.
rows.outlook: Reuters reports markets broadly expect a rate hike at the Fed's Dec. 8-9 meeting and further increases next year.
rows.why: 물가가 잡히지 않을 때 중앙은행이 '기다리는 것'에도 비용이 있다는 논리를 통해, 통화정책의 시차와 선제 대응의 의미를 배울 수 있습니다.
rows.why_en: Her argument that waiting also has a cost teaches how policy lags work and why central banks sometimes act before inflation gets worse.
rows.term_def: When a central bank reacts too slowly to rising inflation, so it has to raise rates more sharply later to catch up.
rows.note: 7-day story (speech delivered Nov. 20 in Santiago). Figures checked against the speech text on federalreserve.gov and Yahoo Finance's report. Separate event from the Fed minutes covered on Nov. 19.

opinion.title: The Global Week Ahead: Caught in the Moment
opinion.author: Derek Holt
opinion.summary: Scotiabank's Derek Holt warns that U.S. inflation readings over the holidays may look hotter than they really are. Retail discounting is much weaker than usual this year, partly because AI-driven demand has pushed up electronics component prices, so the usual seasonal adjustments that offset holiday sales could inflate the adjusted figures. He adds that El Niño weather effects are probably also lifting prices for now but should fade. Holt argues the Fed should look through at least some of this temporary wave, though he admits that is hard, and he sees a risk of the committee overreacting. He expects October core PCE of roughly 0.3% a month, which would back the case for another hike on Dec. 9.
opinion.why: 같은 물가 지표라도 계절조정 방식에 따라 실제보다 높게 보일 수 있다는 점을 알려주며, Cook 이사의 매파적 주장과 균형 있게 비교해 볼 수 있습니다.
opinion.why_en: It shows how seasonal adjustment can make inflation look higher than it is, giving a useful counterweight to Cook's hawkish case.

rows.title: KOSPI rout fuels calls for bolder stabilization measures
rows.summary: South Korea's top economic officials held an emergency meeting on Sunday, Nov. 22, after the KOSPI plunged 5.21% on Friday to 4,869.96, its first close below 4,900 in about 10 months, as doubts about returns on AI investment hit chip stocks. Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il, Bank of Korea Governor Shin Hyun-song and the heads of the Financial Services Commission and Financial Supervisory Service agreed to prepare to activate the stock market stabilization fund if needed. They also agreed to ease limits on companies buying back their own shares for three months and to step up surveillance of illegal short selling for three months. Short selling on the KOSPI and Kosdaq totalled 21.6 trillion won over 14 sessions this month, with foreign investors making up about 75% of it, but Korea has held back from new short-selling curbs partly because such rules were cited as a hurdle to developed-market status in MSCI indexes. Critics, including opposition lawmakers, say the measures so far have done little to calm the market.
rows.fact: The KOSPI fell 5.21% on Nov. 20 and 7.95% over the week. On Nov. 22 officials agreed to prepare the stabilization fund for possible use, ease share-buyback limits for three months and intensify monitoring of illegal short selling for three months.
rows.outlook: Citi Korea's Kim Jin-wook said that simply signalling the fund could be used might discourage short sellers even before any money is deployed.
rows.why: 정부가 주식시장 급락에 어떤 수단(안정기금, 자사주 매입 완화, 공매도 감시)으로 대응하는지, 그리고 시장 개입의 장단점을 배울 수 있습니다.
rows.why_en: It shows the tools a government uses when stock prices crash, such as a stabilization fund, buyback easing and short-selling checks, and the trade-offs of stepping in.
rows.term_def: Borrowing shares and selling them, hoping to buy them back later at a lower price. It can profit from falling prices but may add to selling pressure in a slump.
rows.note: Today's policy (emergency meeting Nov. 22 KST). Measures cross-checked with SBS and Seoul Economic Daily reports of the same meeting; SBS says the fund currently totals 10.76 trillion won. Different event from the Nov. 21 story on foreign selling in October.

opinion.title: Taiwan, China tap market rescue funds. Why won't Korea?
opinion.author: Lee Yeon-woo
opinion.summary: This analysis asks why Korea had not used its market stabilization fund while China and Taiwan tapped theirs after a post-U.S.-midterm sell-off. It notes Korea has created such funds several times but has not actually deployed one since 2008, while Taiwan has used its fund 10 times since 2000, according to Floodlines Research founder Anna Wu, who calls Korea's fund a last bullet. President Lee Jae Myung had said in October that direct intervention would be undesirable, though some market experts argued it may be needed. Emmer Capital's Manishi Raychaudhuri says a fund would need to be well above 20 trillion won, ideally 25 to 30 trillion, to matter in a market worth about 3,000 trillion won. Analysts quoted warn that any boost from intervention may be short-lived.
opinion.why: 정부의 시장 개입이 효과를 내려면 규모와 신호가 얼마나 중요한지, 다른 나라 사례와 비교해 생각해 볼 수 있는 분석입니다.
opinion.why_en: Comparing Korea with Taiwan and China, it shows why the size of a rescue fund and the signal it sends both matter.

rows.title: EU budget: Costa pitches more cuts, Big Tech tax to break deadlock
rows.summary: European Council President António Costa proposed a 2028-2034 EU budget of about €1.78 trillion, roughly 10% or €204 billion less than the European Commission's nearly €2 trillion plan. The cuts reach cohesion and farm spending, competitiveness and defence, external action and administration, going beyond an earlier compromise from the Irish presidency. To raise new money of its own, the EU would add a 3% levy on large digital firms' net revenue from online ads, online intermediation and user data, applied only above €750 million in global turnover and €50 million in EU turnover. Other new revenue would come from a share of carbon-market income, higher minimum tobacco taxes, a plastic levy and the carbon border tax, worth about €64 billion a year in total. France said the plan is not a basis for agreement, while frugal states such as Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden had wanted much deeper cuts, ahead of a leaders' summit on Nov. 26-27.
rows.fact: Costa's draft sets the 2028-2034 budget at about €1.78 trillion, a €204 billion cut from the Commission's proposal. It adds a 3% digital services levy and other new revenues totalling about €64 billion a year.
rows.outlook: Euronews suggests a Trump administration weakened by its midterm defeat may be less inclined to retaliate against the digital levy.
rows.why: 27개국이 함께 쓰는 예산을 누가 얼마나 내고 어디에 쓸지 다투는 과정을 통해, 재정 분담과 디지털세 같은 새로운 세금의 쟁점을 배울 수 있습니다.
rows.why_en: Watching 27 countries argue over who pays and what gets funded explains burden-sharing and the debate over new taxes such as a digital levy.
rows.term_def: The EU's own sources of revenue, such as customs duties or new levies, as opposed to money paid in by member governments from their national budgets.
rows.note: Latest policy (proposal presented Nov. 21, 13:29 CET). Euronews figures are nominal; 2025-price figures elsewhere (about €1.58 trillion) are lower. Key points cross-checked with TRT World's AFP report.

opinion.title: EU enlargement and external action are the sacrificial lambs of Costa's 2028-2034 MFF nego box
opinion.author: The New Union Post
opinion.summary: This analysis argues that the EU's foreign-policy spending takes some of the biggest hits in Costa's plan. It says the Global Europe external-action budget is cut by about 21% from the Commission's proposal, a deeper cut than in earlier drafts from the Cypriot and Irish presidencies. The pillar for enlargement and the EU's eastern neighbours falls to €30.9 billion from €38.1 billion. By contrast, the reserve for Ukraine stays unchanged at up to €88.8 billion, plus up to €42.6 billion in budget guarantees. The piece calls the overall 10% cut the thorniest issue and says reaching a deal by year-end will be challenging.
opinion.why: 예산을 줄일 때 어떤 분야가 먼저 깎이는지를 보여주어, 정부 예산이 곧 우선순위의 선택이라는 점을 이해하게 해줍니다.
opinion.why_en: By showing which areas get cut first, it makes clear that a budget is really a set of choices about priorities.

rows.title: Bank of Japan to raise interest rates in December and again by end-March, economists say: Reuters poll
rows.summary: A Reuters poll of economists taken Nov. 11-18 found that 86% expect the Bank of Japan to raise its policy rate by a quarter point to 1.50% at its Dec. 17-18 meeting. That would be the BOJ's third hike this year, the first time in 37 years it has raised rates three times in one calendar year. Nearly 60% expect another increase to 1.75% by the end of March, three months earlier than in the previous poll. The survey followed Governor Kazuo Ueda's comment on Nov. 18 that the bank should keep raising rates, after core inflation moved back above 2%. The poll comes even though Japan's economy shrank in July-September and the yen sits near 160 per dollar despite heavy government intervention.
rows.fact: In the Reuters poll, 61 of 71 economists expect a December hike to 1.50%, and 35 of 61 expect a rise to 1.75% by end-March. Ueda said on Nov. 18 that the BOJ should continue raising interest rates.
rows.outlook: Economists split evenly on where hikes will stop, with 48% seeing 1.75% as the peak and an equal share expecting 2% or higher.
rows.why: 수십 년간 초저금리를 유지하던 일본이 금리를 연달아 올리는 이유와, 엔화 약세·물가가 금리 결정에 어떤 영향을 주는지 배울 수 있습니다.
rows.why_en: It explains why Japan, after decades of near-zero rates, keeps raising them, and how a weak yen and inflation shape that decision.
rows.term_def: The highest level a central bank's policy rate is expected to reach before the bank stops raising it.
rows.note: 7-day story (poll published Nov. 19 Tokyo). Distinct from the Japan October CPI release covered on Nov. 20; this piece covers the BOJ's rate path and Ueda's Nov. 18 remarks.

opinion.title: Analysis-BOJ locks in December hike, but neutral-rate uncertainty muddies outlook
opinion.author: Leika Kihara
opinion.summary: This Reuters analysis says the BOJ has effectively signalled a December hike to 1.5% from 1.25%, after declaring that its long battle to reach its 2% price target had moved into a new phase focused on avoiding an overshoot. The harder question is how far rates should go, because BOJ staff estimate the neutral rate somewhere between 1.1% and 2.5%. Board members differ: one hawk sees neutral near 2%, while two doves appointed by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi opposed the September hike. Former BOJ official Nobuyasu Atago called a December hike pretty much a done deal. Nomura's Mari Iwashita expects the rate to reach 1.75% by around March, followed by a possible pause.
opinion.why: 경제를 과열시키지도 식히지도 않는 '중립금리'를 정확히 알 수 없다는 점이 왜 중앙은행의 가장 큰 고민인지 보여주는 분석입니다.
opinion.why_en: It shows why not knowing the exact neutral rate, the level that neither speeds up nor slows the economy, is a central bank's biggest headache.
